product.title: Cantonese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twelve Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero in Hong Kong Cantonese: Jyutping printed right above the traditional characters, short natural dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Cantonese builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, interactive exercises, and an answer key. Includes a Jyutping chart, six-tone practice, classifiers, sentence-final particles, an A1 grammar summary, and the first 150 characters. Each unit targets one of the spots learners most often get wrong — including the habit of slipping Mandarin words into Cantonese sentences.

cover_design.label: CANTONESE
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Cantonese for complete beginners — from greeting people and haggling in Mongkok to ordering at a cha chaan teng and talking about yesterday.
cover_design.catatan: Jyutping printed above every character, a word-for-word translation under every line of dialogue.

blocks.text: Cantonese is often introduced the wrong way: as a “dialect of Mandarin”. It isn't. Cantonese and Mandarin are both Chinese languages, use the same family of characters, and share many words — but put side by side, their speakers can't understand each other. The gap is roughly like Spanish and Italian: one family, two languages.

What makes Cantonese appealing to learn is the part people rarely mention. **Its grammar is remarkably simple.** Verbs never change form. No *am / is / are*, no third-person -s, no past tense, no plurals, no grammatical gender. 我去 *ngo5 heoi3* = I go; 佢去 *keoi5 heoi3* = he goes; 琴日我去 *kam4 jat6 ngo5 heoi3* = yesterday I went. The verb is exactly the same in all three sentences.

Only two things are hard: **tones** and **characters**. Cantonese has six tones — two more than Mandarin — and uses traditional characters with denser strokes. This course handles both differently from most books. Tones are practiced from the first page, not parked in an introductory chapter and forgotten. Characters are never left bare — Jyutping is printed **right above them**, so you can read full sentences from Unit 1 without memorizing a single character first.

There's one more thing that's typically Cantonese and almost always skipped by beginner books: **sentence-final particles**. 啦、㗎、喎、咋、囉、添 — one syllable at the end that turns a flat sentence friendly, complaining, surprised, or insistent. A foreigner with perfect grammar who doesn't use particles sounds like a polite robot. This course adds them little by little from Unit 3, instead of piling them into one chapter at the back.

The twelve units in this course aren't a random list of topics. Each unit targets one of the spots learners most often get wrong: 係 used in the wrong place, 好 mistaken for “very”, 咗 mistaken for a past tense, skipped classifiers, and the habit of slipping Mandarin words learned earlier into Cantonese sentences. These spots aren't fixed with memorized rules, but with sentences said over and over until the wrong version feels strange.

How to use it: one unit per sitting, twenty to thirty minutes. Read the dialogues out loud — out loud, not in your head. Cantonese is a language whose meanings live in the rise and fall of your voice, and you can't train that with your eyes.
Enjoy your studies. 加油 — *gaa1 jau2*, you can do it.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones set up.

blocks.text: This course is designed for self-study, with no teacher beside you. Every unit has the same layout, so after Unit 2 you won't need to think about how to study anymore — you just study.
How each unit is laid out

items: **對話 — Dialogue.** Short, natural conversations, not made-up example sentences. Each line has three layers: traditional characters with Jyutping above them, a readable English translation, and a **literal translation** showing the original structure word by word.
**Notes.** Explanations of the things in the dialogue that will make you wonder. They come after the dialogue, not before, so you ask first and get the answer second.
**Grammar boxes.** One pattern, one box. Tables and examples, not grammar jargon.
**Extra sections.** Things you need that aren't grammar: money, numbers, manners, how to survive real situations in Hong Kong.
**Vocabulary in this unit.** Every new word in the unit, with Jyutping and meaning.
**Exercises + answer key.** Six exercises, with the answers right below. Do them first, then check the key — a key you peeked at first teaches you nothing.
**Wave review.** One short task that brings earlier units back to the surface.

blocks.text: The rules that really make the difference

items: **Read aloud.** Cantonese tells meanings apart by tone, and it has six of them. A tone you only read in your head never makes it to your mouth. If you can only pick one rule from this list, pick this one.
**One unit a day, not two.** What counts isn't how long you sit, but how many days in a row you sit. Twenty minutes every day beats three hours once a week, and by no small margin.

**Don't memorize the characters in Unit 1.** Read through the Jyutping first. The characters will stick on their own because the same words keep coming back — and by Unit 5 you'll notice you already recognize some without ever sitting down to memorize them.
**Cover the meaning column.** A vocabulary list you only read left to right teaches you nothing. Cover the English column, read the characters, say the meaning out loud.

**If you've studied Mandarin, watch out for your old habits.** This is your biggest advantage and your biggest trap: the characters look alike, so you'll be tempted to read them with Mandarin sounds and use Mandarin words Hongkongers don't use. Each unit flags those spots with ⚠️.

blocks.title: Three symbols used throughout the course
items: ⚠️ — the spots people get wrong most often. If you only have time for some of the notes, read these.
🇭🇰 — real Hong Kong habits: what people actually say, not what the book says they should.
🔁 — comes back later. No need to master it yet.

front.title: Jyutping: reading the sounds of Cantonese

blocks.text: Jyutping (粵拼 *jyut6 ping3*) is a way of writing Cantonese sounds in the Latin alphabet, created by the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong in 1993. It's used throughout this course and in almost every modern Cantonese dictionary. The number after each syllable is its tone, not part of its sound: *hou2* is read “hou” with tone number 2.
Most Jyutping letters are read roughly as an English speaker would guess. Only a handful below need learning.
Letters that aren't read the way you'd guess

head: Jyutping
Sounds like
Example
rows: like an unaspirated **j / ts** — between *j* and *ch*, no puff of air
like **ch** or **ts**, with a puff of air
rounded-lip vowels that English doesn't have (like French *u*, *eu*)
a real **ng** sound at the start of a word, as in *singer*

blocks.title: Three pairs people mix up most
items: **aa vs a** — [三|saam1] *saam1* (three) ≠ [心|sam1] *sam1* (heart). The first holds its a twice as long.
**z vs c** — [做|zou6] *zou6* (do) ≠ [粗|cou1] *cou1* (rough). The only difference is the puff of air after the letter; hold your palm in front of your mouth and feel it.
**n- vs l-** 🇭🇰 — [你|nei5] *nei5* (you) is said **lei5** by a great many Hongkongers every day. Both are correct and understood; this course writes n- because that's the dictionary form.

blocks.text: Held syllable endings

Cantonese keeps three final sounds Mandarin has lost: **-p, -t, -k**. Syllables ending this way always carry tone 1, 3, or 6, and the sound stops abruptly — like the *p* in a clipped “yep!” where the lips close but never release.

blocks.title: The most useful five-minute drill
items: Read this sequence out loud ten times, slowly at first: *jat1 · ji6 · saam1 · sei3 · ng5 · luk6 · cat1 · baat3 · gau2 · sap6*. Those are the numbers one to ten, and all six Cantonese tones are already in there.
Then record yourself on your phone and listen. Your ears catch tone mistakes your mouth doesn't notice.

blocks.text: Cantonese has six tones. If you've heard the number nine, that's a traditional count that splits off three tones on syllables ending in -p/-t/-k as their own category; the sounds are still six. Cantonese tones are flatter than Mandarin's — what sets them apart is mainly **pitch height**, not rise and fall.
Picture a pitch scale numbered from 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest). The six Cantonese tones sit at different heights on that scale.

head: Tone
Contour
Example
Meaning
rows: high, level — like a phone's ringtone
rising from mid to high — like asking “yeah?”
mid, level — your normal speaking voice
low, falling slightly — like a sigh

blocks.title: What really matters at the start
items: **First tell apart high (1) — mid (3) — low (6).** All three are level; only the pitch differs. Once these three are solid, the rest follow: tone 2 rises to 1, tone 5 rises to 3, tone 4 falls below 6.

⚠️ **Don't copy Mandarin tones.** Mandarin tone 2 jumps sharply; Cantonese tone 2 rises more briefly and stops lower. Mandarin tone 4 falls hard; Cantonese tone 4 is actually the lowest and barely moves.

**Sing them, don't memorize them.** [九|gau2] *gau2* (nine) and [狗|gau2] *gau2* (dog) happen to be the same; but [媽|maa1] (mother), [馬|maa5] (horse), and [罵|maa6] (scold) are not. Say those three words in a row every day for a week.

blocks.text: Tones that change on their own

🇭🇰 Everyday Cantonese often raises the last syllable of a word to **tone 2**, especially for familiar everyday things. This is called a changed tone (變調 *bin3 diu6*), and this course writes the form people actually say, not the dictionary form.

Hong Kong uses **traditional characters** (繁體字 *faan4 tai2 zi6*), not the simplified characters used in mainland China. 學 not 学, 飲 not 饮, 錢 not 钱. They have more strokes, but they're actually easier to tell apart — and they're closer to the characters you'll see in Taiwan, in old texts, and on old shop signs.

Cantonese also has **characters of its own** that don't exist in Mandarin at all. These aren't typos; they're Cantonese words written with characters created for them, and nearly all use the 口 (mouth) component on the left as a marker for “this is a Cantonese sound”.

blocks.title: Three things to know before you start
items: **Spoken Cantonese and written Cantonese are two different things.** Newspapers and official letters in Hong Kong are written in standard Mandarin grammar and read aloud with Cantonese sounds. This course teaches **spoken** Cantonese — the language of WhatsApp, menu boards, and everyday conversation. That's what you need in order to speak.

⚠️ **If you've studied Mandarin**, the table above is a list of habits to hold back. Saying 我是印尼人 in Hong Kong will be understood but sounds like reading from a book; what people say is [我係印尼人|ngo5 hai6 jan3 nei4 jan4].

**You don't need to be able to write characters to finish this course.** The A1 goal is recognizing and saying them. Handwriting can come later at any time — and in Hong Kong itself, nearly everyone types characters on their phone via Jyutping.

blocks.text: All the grammar set up in the twelve units of this course, gathered in one place. These pages aren't for reading once from top to bottom, but for coming back to whenever you're unsure.
Basic sentence order

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: [琴日我去咗旺角|kam4 jat6 ngo5 heoi3 zo2 wong6 gok3]。
[我喺屋企食飯|ngo5 hai2 uk1 kei2 sik6 faan6]。

blocks.text: Six ways to ask questions

head: Method
Example
Note
rows: [你係唔係學生|nei5 hai6 m4 hai6 hok6 saang1]？
The most common. The verb is repeated with 唔 in between.
[你食咗飯未呀|nei5 sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6 aa3]？
Softens a question rather than making one.
The question word stands **where the answer goes**; it doesn't move to the front.
[佢返咗嚟未|keoi5 faan1 zo2 lei4 mei6]？
[聽日得唔得|ting1 jat6 dak1 m4 dak1]？

blocks.text: Marking time without changing the verb
Cantonese has no past tense. Instead it uses aspect markers — one syllable attached after the verb to describe the **state** of the action, not when it happened.

head: Marker
Meaning
Example
rows: [我去過|ngo5 heoi3 gwo3]。 I've been there.
[食晒|sik6 saai3]。 Eat it all up.
[我未食|ngo5 mei6 sik6]。 I haven't eaten yet.

blocks.text: Sentence-final particles

head: Particle
What it adds
Example
rows: [佢係老師㗎|keoi5 hai6 lou5 si1 gaa3]。 He really is a teacher.
[落雨喎|lok6 jyu5 wo3]。 Oh, it's raining.
[十蚊咋|sap6 man1 zaa3]。 Only ten dollars.
[咁咪去囉|gam2 mai6 heoi3 lo1]。 Well, just go then.
[要多一杯添|jiu3 do1 jat1 bui1 tim1]。 One more glass, please.
[佢好好人嘅|keoi5 hou2 hou2 jan4 ge3]。 He really is a good person.

blocks.text: Much as English says *a cup of*, *a sheet of*, *a head of*, Cantonese inserts a classifier between a number and its noun. The difference: in Cantonese it's **required**, and the classifier is also used without a number to mean “the”.

head: Classifier
Used for
Example
rows: people, general things — if unsure, use this
flat things: paper, tables, cards, chairs
[一杯茶|jat1 bui1 caa4] a glass of tea
[兩碗飯|loeng5 wun2 faan6] two bowls of rice
long things: streets, pants, fish, keys
rooms and buildings: shops, houses, schools
[一間舖頭|jat1 gaan1 pou3 tau2] a shop

blocks.title: Three lifesavers
items: **The number “two” changes before a classifier.** [二|ji6] is only for counting and numbers. For two of something, use [兩|loeng5]: [兩個人|loeng5 go3 jan4], not 二個人.
**A classifier with no number = “the”.** [本書|bun2 syu1] means “the book”, one we both know. It replaces the word “the” and is used very often.
⚠️ **Don't put Mandarin 的 between the classifier and the noun.** [兩個人|loeng5 go3 jan4] — nothing comes between 個 and 人.

blocks.text: The characters that appear most often in this course, in the order they first appear. If you recognize them all, you can read most menu boards, MTR signs, and everyday WhatsApp messages in Hong Kong.

If you've reached this page after working through all twelve units, you now have real A1 Cantonese: you can introduce yourself, haggle, order food, ask for directions, make plans, and tell people what you did yesterday. That's not a little — it's the point where a language starts to become usable for learning the language itself.
Three habits that matter most from here

items: **Listen to Cantonese every day, even when you don't understand.** Your ears need time to stop hearing “foreign noise” and start hearing words. Twenty minutes a day is enough; what counts is every day, not how long.

**Repeat it, don't just watch.** Take one sentence from whatever you're listening to, replay it, and copy it until the rhythm matches. It's the only practice that truly moves tones from your head to your mouth.

**Use the particles.** Your grammar is already good enough to be understood; what makes you sound like a person and not a book is 啦、㗎、呀、喎 at the end of the sentence. Copy them from real people, not from a list.

For after A2 — but start listening now as background sound.

A must. Look up characters by handwriting, hear the sound, save to a list.

blocks.title: If you want to keep going with Linguo
items: Linguo's Cantonese classes pick up exactly where this leaves off: A2 starts by expanding compound sentences, longer stories about the past, and everyday Cantonese for work.

Private classes suit you if you have a clear reason — a job move to Hong Kong, a Cantonese-speaking family, or preparing for university. Group classes suit you if what you need is scheduled speaking time.
Bring this book to your first class. Your teacher will know exactly what you already have and pick up from there, not start over.
